summary: Sacks is skeptical of OpenAI's trajectory, citing its shift from nonprofit to aggressive for-profit behavior, co-founder departures, and demands that new investors not fund rival AI companies as red flags.
quote: They originally started that enterprise with $50 million or so from Elon. It was a nonprofit. Then they became a for-profit. Now there's a report saying that they're telling investors in this round that they can't invest in any other AI com

summary: Mark Cuban argues OpenAI's restrictive investor terms reflect fear of competition, not strength, and that Google (Gemini), Meta (open source), and others are serious rivals that make OpenAI's dominance far from certain.
quote: There is no, you know, there's nothing that says that OpenAI is going to win, nothing at all. And so I don't feel bad about what they're doing. And to me, it tells me they're more scared than anything by trying to restrict what people are doing.

summary: Mark Cuban argues X is a structurally challenged advertising business: its embrace of extreme free speech drove away major advertisers, and the proliferation of hate speech and adult content makes the platform toxic for brands, undermining its revenue model.
quote: There is no upside for being on Twitter right now, or X right now. And you add to that the porn. Kids 13 years old can go on that site and you can find any insane thing you want on X right now. And that also is a problem for advertisers.

summary: Mark Cuban co-invested in Groq alongside Chamath, viewing AI infrastructure ('picks and shovels') as the most attractive place to invest in the current AI gold rush.
quote: So now I've kind of slowed down. I invested in Groq, right, with Chamath, right? Chamath is like, yeah, let's go, right? And he can tell you all the reasons.

summary: Mark Cuban argues that Trump's 2020 deal with Saudi Arabia and Russia to cut oil production by 10% drove up the price of oil and gas over two years, contributing directly to the 9.1% inflation peak in 2022. He also notes oil prices are a global phenomenon and domestic production cuts alone don't fully drive domestic gas prices.
quote: what he did, he said, okay, MBS owes me a favor over in Saudi Arabia... And so by reducing production over a plan of 2 years... that increased the price of gas, the price of oil, the price of energy. And that was bad for American consumers

summary: Friedberg pushes back on oil being the primary domestic inflation driver, noting that more than half of US crude oil production is exported, meaning production cuts would have primarily affected exporter profits rather than domestic energy costs.
quote: US crude oil production chart, and more than half of this oil is exported. So you can see the reduction in production, but the domestic oil production capacity remained high relative to our consumption... it really would've affected the profits of the exporting companies, not necessarily the cost of energy domestically.
